notes.claim: A driven RLC series circuit is the electrical analog of a driven damped harmonic oscillator, so one family of ideas covers springs and circuits.
The time constant of an RL circuit is L divided by R, and the current covers 0.632 of the remainder to its final value in every time constant.
Newton's law of cooling gives the rate of cooling of a liquid as proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings' temperature.
The slope of the solution curve through a point is set by the equation itself, as y′ = f(x, y) at that point.
Separation of variables rearranges the equation so every term in the unknown is on one side and every term in the independent variable is on the other.
Radioactive atoms decay exponentially, at a rate that depends on the decay constant.
In an RC circuit the charge and discharge are exponential in time, and the time constant RC sets the pace.
When a coil's supply is switched off, its current falls to 0.368 of the preceding value in each successive time constant.
An exponential never exactly reaches its final value, but covers 0.632 of what remains in every time constant.
Reactor period is the time for reactor power to change by a factor of e, so a reactor's power grows exponentially (added for i2: the plus-sign example).
When a coil is switched onto a supply, the current starts at zero and approaches V divided by R, with a characteristic time constant for an RL circuit.
The time constant for an RL circuit is defined as L divided by R.
The current covers 0.632 of the remainder to its final value in every time constant.
A driven damped system's general solution is a transient that depends on the starting conditions plus a steady state that depends only on the drive.
The first-order Nomoto steering model links a ship's rudder angle to its heading with two parameters, a gain K and a time constant T (added for i3: a ship answering its rudder).
For an RC circuit, the steady-state solution with a single-frequency input voltage gives the same result as the impedance method (added for i3: the sine input).
Euler's method approximates the solution of an initial value problem by following tangent lines, taking horizontal steps across the t-axis.
The slope of the solution curve at each point is set by the equation, and Euler's method uses that slope for each step.
A smaller step gives a better approximation and a larger step a worse one.
A naval teaching paper works out a submarine's dive by stepping its equation with the Euler-Cromer method, a close cousin of Euler's method (added for i4).
In an RLC circuit and a damped spring, the mass behaves the same as an inductor and the spring the same as an inverse capacitance.
An RLC circuit's free oscillations have three cases, all analogous to the cases of a damped spring-mass system.
A driven RLC series circuit is the electrical analog of the driven damped harmonic oscillator.
An RLC circuit's free oscillations have three cases, all analogous to the cases of a damped spring-mass system.
A damped spring has three cases, told apart by the sign of the expression under the square root in the roots of its characteristic equation.
Over-damped, the response looks like an exponential decay back to equilibrium.
Under-damped, the position is a decaying oscillation whose amplitude shrinks until equilibrium is reached.
Critically damped, the position returns to equilibrium in the shortest time, with one or no oscillations.
For fixed m and k, choosing the damping to be the critical value gives the fastest return of the system to equilibrium.
A ship's roll, with damping and restoring moments that are not in step for all angles, is a second-order nonlinear equation, so the straight equation fits only small rolls (added for i6: ship roll).
Measured roll decay of ship models is fitted by an exponentially decaying cosine, the underdamped answer (added for i6: ship roll).
A ship's roll damping increases with forward speed (added for i6: ship roll).
A system in simple harmonic motion has maximum amplitude oscillations when the frequency of the forcing function equals the natural frequency of the system.
A driven damped oscillator's general solution is a transient that depends on the starting conditions plus a steady state that depends only on the driving amplitude.
The resonance effect occurs only in underdamped systems.
More damping reduces the roll amplitude at resonance, though resonance can still occur.
A driven RLC series circuit is the electrical analog of the driven damped harmonic oscillator, so circuits resonate as springs do.

Bilge keels are one of the devices that reduce a ship's roll; damping stabilization adds damping, sometimes with appendages on the hull, and so reduces the resonant peak (added for i7: the bilge keels puzzle).
A ship's roll can be large, even enough to capsize it, when the waves come too close to its natural roll frequency (added for i7: why roll resonance matters).
